q: I created ~/.bash_profile and now my aliases are gone over SSH. Why?
expl: Bash reads only the first of `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login`, `~/.profile`. Source `~/.profile` from `~/.bash_profile` to fix it.
opts: SSH never reads any startup file
A login shell now reads ~/.bash_profile and skips ~/.profile, so ~/.bashrc never loads

q: Where should an alias go so every new terminal tab has it?
expl: A new tab is an interactive, non-login shell, and it reads only `~/.bashrc`. Keep environment variables in `~/.profile`.

q: You added an alias to `~/.bashrc`. Type the command that loads the change into the shell you are already in.
expl: `source` (or its short form `.`) runs the file in the current shell. `bash ~/.bashrc` runs it in a child shell, and the alias dies with it.

q: Type a `bash` command that starts a login shell (like SSH does) and only runs `true`.
expl: `-l` (or `--login`) makes bash a login shell, so it reads the login files: here `~/.profile`.

q: You create `~/.bash_profile` with just one line, `export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"`. Which of your startup files does a login shell read now?
expl: A login shell stops at the first file it finds, so `~/.profile` (and the `~/.bashrc` it loads) is skipped.

q: With the demo user's files (an echo line at the top of `~/.bashrc` and of `~/.profile`, no `~/.bash_profile`), what does this print?
expl: An interactive non-login shell, like a new terminal tab, reads only `~/.bashrc`.

q: Same demo user. What does a login shell print?
expl: The login shell reads `~/.profile`, and Debian's default `~/.profile` then loads `~/.bashrc`.

q: Why does a login shell on Debian also get your aliases from `~/.bashrc`?
expl: Look for the `BASH_VERSION` block in `~/.profile`: it sources `~/.bashrc`. That's why the chain breaks when `~/.profile` is skipped.
opts: Bash always reads every startup file
Debian's default `~/.profile` has a few lines that load `~/.bashrc` when the shell is bash

q: Your `~/.bash_profile` exists and login shells lost your aliases. Which line do you add to it?
expl: Loading `~/.profile` from `~/.bash_profile` brings back the chain: `~/.bash_profile` → `~/.profile` → `~/.bashrc`.

q: Where do environment variables like `PATH` or `EDITOR` belong?
expl: `~/.profile` is read by login shells (bash and also plain `sh`), and the variables are inherited by everything started from there.
